title: Water Tank Capacity Calculator | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Calculate Water Tank Capacity by Number of People
description: Find the right water tank size for any home or project. Enter residents and backup days for instant, accurate capacity results.
intro:
Choosing the wrong water tank size is one of the most common—and costly—mistakes in residential and commercial construction. Too small, and your household runs dry during municipal supply interruptions or peak demand periods. Too large, and you waste money on materials, installation, and the structural reinforcement needed to support excess weight. The consequences go beyond inconvenience: stagnant water in oversized tanks promotes bacterial growth, including *Legionella* and coliform bacteria, while undersized tanks leave families without water during emergencies, pressure drops, or scheduled maintenance cuts.

The industry standard for daily residential water consumption is **200 liters (53 US gallons) per person per day**, a figure endorsed by the World Health Organization (WHO) for basic sanitation adequacy and used as the baseline by plumbing codes across North America, Europe, and Latin America. However, real-world usage varies significantly: a household with low-flow fixtures, water-efficient appliances, and conscious conservation habits may use as little as 120–150 liters per person, while a home with a garden irrigation system, a pool top-up line, or multiple bathrooms in simultaneous use can exceed 300 liters per person daily.

Backup reserve days are equally critical. Urban properties connected to a reliable municipal network typically size for **1 day of autonomy**—enough to bridge a standard overnight or weekend maintenance window. Suburban and peri-urban homes, where supply interruptions can last 24–48 hours without warning, should plan for **2–3 days**. Rural properties on well systems or areas prone to infrastructure failures may need **4–7 days** of stored capacity, especially if the household includes vulnerable members who depend on uninterrupted water access for medical reasons.

This calculator applies the universally accepted formula—**Capacity (L) = People × Daily consumption (L) × Reserve days**—to give you an immediate, actionable tank size. It's designed for homeowners planning a new build or renovation, plumbing contractors verifying system specs, civil engineering students working through hydraulic design problems, and anyone who needs a fast sanity check before ordering equipment. No sign-up, no software to install, no waiting: enter your two inputs and get your answer in seconds, with enough context to make a confident decision or bring a well-informed question to your licensed plumber or structural engineer.
keyTakeaway: Formula: **L = people × 200 × reserve days**. Direct calculation from your inputs. Tank capacity based on occupants and backup days.

explanation:
## How Water Tank Capacity Is Calculated

Residential water tank capacity is determined by occupant count and desired backup supply duration. This calculator applies the formula with your inputs, checks reasonable ranges, and alerts you to unusual values.

## Key Factors

- **Daily consumption**: 200 liters per person is the standard allocation
- **Reserve days**: 1 day for urban areas with reliable supply; 2–3 days for suburban or rural properties
- **Tank material**: High-density polyethylene (triple-wall) is most common and durable
- **Installation**: Always on a solid, level base. Never directly on soft soil
- **Water pressure**: Tank positioned 8–10 meters above fixtures ensures adequate pressure

## Final Notes

This calculation is a reference guide only. For critical decisions (building permits, system design, code compliance), consult a licensed plumber or engineer. Values are current to 2026 and reviewed regularly.

faq.q: How much water does one person actually use per day, and where does the 200-liter figure come from?
faq.a: The 200-liter (53 US gallon) per-person-per-day figure is the internationally recognized standard for residential water consumption in urban settings with full plumbing infrastructure. It accounts for drinking (2–3 L), cooking (5–10 L), toilet flushing (30–50 L), showering (60–80 L), laundry (30–50 L), dishwashing (15–25 L), and general cleaning. The World Health Organization (WHO) uses this benchmark in its sanitation planning guidelines. In practice, consumption varies: water-efficient households with low-flow fixtures typically consume 120–150 L per person per day, while homes with gardens, pools, or high-occupancy bathrooms may reach 250–350 L. For the most accurate sizing, track your household's actual water meter readings over 30 days and divide by the number of residents.

faq.q: How many backup days should I plan for, and what factors influence that decision?
faq.a: The right number of backup days depends on the reliability of your water source and the consequences of running dry. Urban properties connected to a consistent municipal network generally size for 1 day—enough to cover overnight maintenance or brief pressure drops. Suburban areas with periodic service interruptions should plan for 2–3 days. Rural properties on well systems, especially those prone to power outages that disable submersible pumps, typically need 3–7 days of stored capacity. Additional factors include whether anyone in the household has medical needs requiring uninterrupted water (dialysis, wound care), whether you have a garden or livestock that can't go without water, and local climate risks like freezes that damage pipes or droughts that reduce well yield. When in doubt, size up: the incremental cost of a larger tank is usually far less than the cost of an emergency water delivery.

faq.q: Should I add a safety margin on top of the calculated capacity, and how much?
faq.a: Yes, most plumbing engineers recommend adding a 10–20% safety margin above the calculated minimum. This buffer accounts for peak-demand days (weekends, holidays, houseguests), seasonal increases in consumption during hot months, the fact that tanks are never fully emptied in practice—water near the outlet valve is typically not usable—and the reality that commercial tanks are sold in fixed increments (500 L, 1,000 L, 1,500 L, 2,000 L, 3,000 L, etc.), so you're always rounding to the next available size anyway. For example, if your calculation yields 1,600 L, the standard recommendation is to purchase a 2,000 L tank rather than trying to combine two smaller units.

faq.q: What are the most common tank materials, and which should I choose?
faq.a: The four main options each have trade-offs. **High-density polyethylene (HDPE or PEAD)**, often marketed as triple-wall or multi-layer tanks, is the most popular choice worldwide: lightweight, UV-resistant, corrosion-proof, easy to install, and available in a wide range of sizes. **Fiberglass (GRP)** tanks are stronger and better suited for underground or semi-buried installations, but cost more and require professional handling. **Stainless steel** tanks are ideal where hygiene is paramount (food service, medical facilities) but are expensive and can sweat condensation. **Reinforced concrete cisterns** are permanent, extremely durable, and cost-effective at large volumes (10,000 L+), but require professional construction and periodic sealing to prevent leaching. For standard residential use, a UV-stabilized polyethylene tank from a reputable manufacturer is the best balance of cost, durability, and ease of maintenance.

faq.q: How high does my tank need to be elevated to achieve good water pressure?
faq.a: Water pressure from a gravity-fed tank is determined entirely by the vertical height (head) between the water surface in the tank and the outlet point. The relationship is: **1 meter of head ≈ 0.098 bar (1.42 psi)**. For acceptable household pressure of 1–2 bar (15–30 psi), your tank water surface needs to be at least 10–20 meters above your fixtures—which is rarely achievable with a rooftop tank on a standard residential building. Most single-family homes achieve only 3–6 meters of head, producing 0.3–0.6 bar, which is adequate for gravity-fed showers and faucets but insufficient for certain appliances (instant water heaters, some washing machines) that require minimum 1.5–2 bar. The solution is a pressure booster pump installed on the outlet line, which is standard in most modern residential systems. Always check the minimum pressure requirements of your appliances before finalizing your installation design.

faq.q: How often should I clean my water storage tank, and what's the correct procedure?
faq.a: Most health authorities and tank manufacturers recommend cleaning and disinfecting residential water tanks every 6–12 months, or immediately after any contamination event (flood, dead animal found in or near the tank, visible algae growth, or unexplained taste/odor changes). The procedure: (1) Shut off the inlet valve and drain the tank completely via the drain cock. (2) Scrub all interior surfaces with a stiff brush and a solution of 1 part household bleach (5.25% sodium hypochlorite) to 100 parts water. (3) Rinse thoroughly with clean water at least twice. (4) Refill and add a final disinfection dose: approximately 1 mL of household bleach per 100 liters of tank capacity. (5) Allow to stand for 30 minutes, then flush the distribution lines by running taps until the chlorine smell dissipates. Keep a cleaning log with dates for maintenance records.

faq.q: What structural considerations apply when installing a large water tank?
faq.a: Water weighs 1 kilogram per liter (1 ton per 1,000 liters), so a full 3,000 L tank weighs approximately 3,050 kg including the tank itself. Before installation, you must verify that the supporting structure can handle this load. Rooftop installations require a structural engineering assessment of the slab's live load capacity—most residential slabs are designed for 150–300 kg/m², which can easily be exceeded by a large tank concentrated on a small footprint. Ground-level tanks need a reinforced concrete pad (typically 15–20 cm thick with rebar) to distribute the load and prevent settling that could crack the tank or stress the inlet/outlet connections. Never place a tank directly on soil, wood, or any surface that could shift or compress unevenly. For tanks larger than 2,000 L, always consult a structural engineer before installation.

faq.q: Can I connect two or more tanks together, and how does that work?
faq.a: Yes, connecting multiple tanks in parallel is a standard solution when your required capacity exceeds what's available in a single unit, or when you want redundancy for maintenance purposes. In a parallel configuration, all tanks share the same inlet and outlet manifolds, effectively acting as one large tank. Use equal-diameter pipes and balanced valve arrangements to ensure all tanks fill and drain at the same rate—otherwise one tank will always be fuller than the others, causing uneven wear and potential overflow. A common practical approach is to install a main distribution manifold with individual shutoff valves for each tank, allowing you to isolate any single tank for cleaning or repair while the others remain in service. Make sure all tanks are installed at exactly the same elevation; even a 2–3 cm height difference will cause flow imbalance in a passive (non-pumped) gravity system.

faq.q: Does water stored in a tank lose quality over time, and how can I prevent it?
faq.a: Yes, stored water degrades over time through several mechanisms. Residual chlorine from municipal treatment dissipates within 24–72 hours, after which bacterial growth is no longer inhibited. UV light penetrating translucent tanks promotes algae growth. Temperature fluctuations cause condensation and promote biofilm formation on tank walls. Sediment from the supply line accumulates at the bottom. To maintain water quality: (1) Use opaque, UV-stabilized tanks—never clear or translucent ones. (2) Ensure the inlet is positioned at the bottom or side so fresh water circulates the entire tank rather than short-circuiting to the outlet. (3) Install a screen or fine filter on the inlet to exclude debris and insects. (4) Maintain a minimum residual chlorine level of 0.2–0.5 mg/L if water is stored for more than 24 hours (a simple pool test kit can measure this). (5) Size your tank appropriately—an oversized tank with low daily turnover is a greater contamination risk than a correctly sized one.

faq.q: Are there local regulations or codes that govern water tank sizing and installation?
faq.a: Yes, and compliance is important both for safety and for insurance/permitting purposes. In the United States, the International Plumbing Code (IPC) and International Residential Code (IRC) provide baseline standards, but requirements vary by state and municipality—always check with your local building department. In Canada, the National Plumbing Code (NPC) applies, with provincial variations. In the UK, the Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 govern tank design and installation to prevent contamination of the public supply. In Australia, the Plumbing Code of Australia (PCA) sets minimum standards. For most residential installations in the US, a permit is required for any new tank installation or significant modification to the plumbing system, and the work must be performed or inspected by a licensed plumber. Permits protect you: unpermitted work can void home insurance and create liability issues if the system fails.

faq.q: How do I calculate the right tank size if my household has non-standard water uses like irrigation, a pool, or livestock?
faq.a: The standard formula (people × 200 L × reserve days) covers only domestic household use. For non-standard loads, calculate each additional demand separately and add it to the base figure. Garden drip irrigation typically uses 1–4 liters per hour per emitter; multiply by the number of emitters and daily run time. A standard garden hose at full flow uses approximately 15–20 liters per minute. Livestock requirements vary widely: a dairy cow needs 80–150 L/day, a horse 25–50 L/day, a sheep or goat 5–15 L/day. Pool top-up depends on evaporation and splash loss, typically 1–3% of pool volume per week in warm climates. Add these figures to your household base, multiply by reserve days, and apply a 15% safety margin. For complex multi-use systems, a licensed plumber or hydraulic engineer can model peak simultaneous demand—the scenario where all uses are active at the same time—which is the true design constraint.

faq.q: What's the difference between a cistern, a water storage tank, and a pressure tank, and which do I need?
faq.a: These terms are often used interchangeably but refer to distinct components. A **water storage tank** (or cistern) is a large-volume container that stores raw supply water—it's what this calculator helps you size. It operates at atmospheric pressure (no pressurization) and relies on gravity or a booster pump to distribute water through the building. A **pressure tank** (also called a pressure vessel or expansion tank) is a small-volume tank (typically 20–200 liters) connected to a pump system; it contains a pre-charged air bladder that maintains system pressure between pump cycles, reducing pump wear and preventing water hammer. Most modern residential systems use both: a large storage tank as the primary reserve, and a small pressure tank paired with a booster pump to maintain consistent distribution pressure. If you're on a municipal supply with adequate pressure and no storage requirements, you may only need a pressure tank. If you have storage needs, size your storage tank first using this calculator, then size your booster pump and pressure tank based on your peak flow rate requirements.
